content: Resistant starch (RS) is a type of starch that is not digested in the small intestine of healthy individuals. Unlike most carbohydrates, such as sugars and rapidly digestible starches, which are absorbed as glucose in the small intestine and used for energy or stored, resistant starch bypasses digestion and reaches the large intestine. There, it behaves like dietary fiber. Resistant starch is classified into four distinct types: 1. RS1: This type of resistant starch is physically inaccessible or indigestible, as found in seeds, legumes, and unprocessed whole grains. 2. RS2: This form occurs naturally in its granular state, such as in uncooked potatoes, green banana flour, and high-amylose corn. 3. RS3: This type is formed when starch-containing foods are cooked and then cooled, such as in bread, cornflakes, and cooked-and-chilled potatoes. It is also referred to as retrograded starch. 4. RS4: These are chemically modified starches designed to resist digestion. They are not naturally occurring and can have a variety of structures. Resistant starch is considered one of the three main types of dietary fiber, alongside soluble and insoluble fibers. Soluble fibers, such as pectins, gums, and mucilages, are found in fruits, vegetables, oats, legumes, and seeds. They can increase the viscosity of intestinal contents, reduce cholesterol absorption, and are fermented by gut bacteria, promoting colon health and enhancing mineral absorption. Insoluble fibers, such as cellulose and lignin, are found in whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and wheat bran. These fibers provide bulk to stool and help maintain regular bowel movements, though many are not fermented. Resistant starch, on the other hand, is naturally insoluble, acts as a prebiotic fiber, and is fermented in the large intestine. Some forms of resistant starch may also be soluble and may or may not have prebiotic properties. Public health experts have identified a significant gap between the amount of fiber consumed by most individuals and the recommended daily intake. For example, the U.S. National Academy of Sciences recommends 38 grams of fiber per day for adult men and 25 grams per day for adult women. Many countries suggest a daily intake of 25–30 grams of fiber. Resistant starch can help bridge this gap by being incorporated into foods without altering their taste or texture. Health Benefits of Resistant Starch Resistant starch is widely recognized as a beneficial carbohydrate by organizations such as the Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the British Nutrition Foundation. The FAO/WHO Expert Consultation on Human Nutrition has highlighted the discovery of resistant starch as a major advancement in understanding the role of carbohydrates in health. Intestinal and Colonic Health Research on natural resistant starches, particularly those derived from high-amylose corn, has demonstrated significant benefits for intestinal and colonic health. Resistant starch promotes the growth of beneficial gut bacteria while inhibiting harmful bacteria. It is fermented in the colon, producing short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as butyrate, which is the primary energy source for colonic cells. Butyrate has anti-inflammatory and anti-carcinogenic properties, supporting colon health and potentially reducing the risk of colorectal cancer. It also lowers intestinal pH and reduces the production of harmful compounds like secondary bile acids, ammonia, and phenols. Additionally, resistant starch has a mild laxative effect, helping to maintain regular bowel movements. Glycemic Management and Blood Sugar Control Resistant starch helps regulate blood sugar levels by increasing insulin sensitivity in healthy individuals. When incorporated into processed foods as a substitute for flour or other rapidly digestible carbohydrates, resistant starch reduces the glycemic impact of the food. This can help lower the risk of type 2 diabetes. Resistant starch has been shown to decrease postprandial glycemic responses in both healthy individuals and diabetics, while also improving insulin sensitivity. Weight Management Resistant starch contributes to weight management through several mechanisms: 1. Fiber Fortification: Adding resistant starch to foods like bread, pasta, and cereal increases their fiber content without affecting taste or texture. The WHO has recognized dietary fiber as a protective factor against weight gain and obesity, likely due to its ability to increase satiety, reduce hunger, and influence hormone secretion related to digestion. 2. Calorie Reduction: Resistant starch provides fewer calories than rapidly digestible carbohydrates. It delivers 2–3 kilocalories per gram, compared to 4 kilocalories per gram for regular starch. 3. Lipid Oxidation: Resistant starch promotes fat oxidation, which may reduce fat accumulation. Clinical trials with high-amylose corn resistant starch have shown increased fat burning after meals and a shift in the body's energy utilization, prioritizing fat over carbohydrates and protein. Energy Management Foods containing resistant starch provide a steady release of energy, helping to balance blood sugar levels and prevent energy fluctuations. Resistant starch releases glucose in the small intestine and fermentation by-products in the large intestine, which serve as energy sources for muscle and fat tissue. This slow energy release results in moderate blood sugar rises and helps mitigate the rapid glycemic spikes associated with processed carbohydrates. Gluten-Free Applications Resistant starch can be used as a substitute for wheat-based products in gluten-free foods. Its fermentation in the colon produces higher levels of butyrate compared to other fibers, which may be beneficial for individuals with celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease due to its anti-inflammatory and anti-carcinogenic properties. In summary, resistant starch offers a range of health benefits, including improved digestive health, better glycemic control, support for weight management, and potential applications in gluten-free diets. Its ability to act as a prebiotic, promote the production of beneficial SCFAs like butyrate, and reduce the glycemic impact of foods makes it a valuable component of a healthy diet.
